text:
Can you write an email to people who didn't renew their farm share? I run a 30-acre vegetable farm and sell 22-week shares that people pick up every Thursday.

Facts:
- Last year 260 households had a share. 97 didn't renew.
- On July 9 a hailstorm destroyed about half our crops. For the next 6 weeks the boxes had about half the usual amount. We didn't offer refunds or credit, and I sent one short email about it.
- A full share is $540 this year, the same as last year.
- This year we've added a second field on higher ground and put up 2 hail nets over our tomatoes and peppers. That cost $31,000.
- Members can now pause up to 2 weeks and get credit for them.
- Sign-up closes March 15. 52 shares are left.

Under 200 words.

Before I draft this, a few questions. Your answers will change what the email says:

1. **Do you know why the 97 left?** Was it a survey, replies, or comments at pickup? If it was mostly the hail and how it was handled, the email should open by owning that. If the reasons were mixed (moved away, too much food, Thursdays didn't work), I'd write it differently and give the new pause option more weight.
2. **Do you want to apologize outright for how the hail weeks were handled?** I mean the missing refunds or credit and the single short email, not the storm itself. Some former members may still be annoyed about it, and naming it plainly is usually what wins people back. I'd like to know how far you're comfortable going.
3. **Are you offering returning members anything,** like a discount, a bonus week, or early pickup? Or should the case rest on the hail nets, the new field and the pause credit? (I won't invent an offer.)
4. **How are those 52 open shares likely to go?** Do they usually sell out before March 15? If so, saying that is honest urgency. If not, I'll leave out any "spots are going fast" line.
5. **What are the farm name, your sign-off name and the sign-up link** (or should I leave placeholders)? And do you address members by first name in emails?

1. 41 of the 97 answered a short survey in the fall. 29 of them said they'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks.
2. Yes, I want to say sorry plainly. I didn't write more after the hail because I was working 16-hour days trying to save what was left.
3. No discount or bonus. But I can commit to a short email to members every Thursday of the season, and a credit for any week when weather cuts a box by more than a third. I can't promise there won't be crop loss this year.
4. I don't know.
5. Greenbank Farm, sign off as Sam Turner. Sign-up is through the link on our website. I don't know about first names, your call.

I've addressed it with a first-name placeholder ("Hi [First name]"), since a personal greeting helps an apology land. I didn't add any urgency beyond the date and the 52 shares left, because you don't know how fast they'll sell. The email is about 185 words.

<final_document>
Subject: We got the hail weeks wrong. Here's what's changed.

Hi [First name],

On July 9, hail destroyed about half our crops. For six weeks your box held about half what it should have, and all you got was one short email and no credit. I'm sorry. I was working 16-hour days trying to save what was left, but you deserved better from us.

Most of you who answered our fall survey said you'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks. Here's what we've changed:

- **Credit for short boxes.** If weather cuts a box by more than a third, you get credit for that week.
- **A weekly update.** I'll email you every Thursday of the season.
- **Less hail risk.** We spent $31,000 on a second field on higher ground and two hail nets over the tomatoes and peppers.
- **Pause weeks.** You can pause up to two weeks and get credit for them.

I can't promise we won't lose crops this year. I can promise you won't be left in the dark again.

A full share is still $540. Sign-up closes March 15, and 52 shares are left. You'll find the link on our website.

Sam Turner
Greenbank Farm
</final_document>
